trip_options.title: Budget Explorer - Lisbon, Portugal
trip_options.description: Save money without sacrificing the experience. Perfect for travelers who value authentic local experiences over luxury.

experiences.name: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour
experiences.description: Spend a few hours grazing through Lisbon's iconic food hall featuring the best local chefs and traditional Portuguese dishes. Sample pastéis de bacalhau, bifanas, ginjinha, and the famous pastel de nata while mingling with locals and learning about Portuguese culinary traditions.

experiences.name: Belém Historical Monuments & Pastéis de Belém
experiences.description: Visit the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery and the iconic Tower of Belém, two masterpieces of Manueline architecture dating back to the Age of Discovery. Afterward, stop at the original Pastéis de Belém bakery, open since 1837, to taste the world-famous custard tarts straight from the source.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear immigration, collect luggage, and take the Metro (Vermelho/Red Line from Aeroporto) to the city centre for around €1.65 using a Viva Viagem card. Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a gentle walk through the historic Baixa (downtown) neighbourhood. Stroll along Rua Augusta, pass through the triumphal arch to Praça do Comércio on the Tagus riverfront — entry is free. Soak in the views of the river and get your bearings in the city.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Alfama district for your first taste of authentic Lisbon. Wander the narrow medieval alleyways and find a spot to listen to live Fado music drifting from small tascas. Grab a seat at a simple local tasca for a budget dinner.

meals.breakfast: Eat on the plane or grab a quick pastel de nata (custard tart, ~€1.20) and a bica (espresso, ~€0.80) at a neighbourhood café near the hotel upon arrival.
meals.lunch: Pick up a prego (steak sandwich) or bifana (pork sandwich) from a local snack bar in Baixa for around €3–5.
meals.dinner: Dine at a traditional tasca in Alfama such as Tasca do Chico or a similar neighbourhood spot. Look for the prato do dia (dish of the day) which typically includes soup, main, bread, and a drink for €8–12.

day_by_day.notes: Buy a 24-hour Viva Viagem card at the airport metro station (€0.50 card + top-up). This covers metro, bus, and tram rides. Tip: avoid the famous Tram 28 on your first evening as it is very crowded with tourists — walk Alfama instead.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) first thing in the morning when crowds are smaller. Entry is €15 for adults but free for EU citizens under 25. Explore the ramparts for panoramic views over Lisbon's terracotta rooftops and the Tagus River. Afterwards, walk down through the atmospheric Mouraria quarter, one of Lisbon's oldest and most multicultural neighbourhoods.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Alfama district in depth — visit the Lisbon Cathedral (Sé de Lisboa), free to enter the main nave. Browse the Feira da Ladra flea market at Campo de Santa Clara (open Tuesdays and Saturdays, free entry) for vintage finds, local crafts, and people-watching. Pick up cheap snacks from market vendors.
day_by_day.evening: Make your way to Miradouro da Graça or Miradouro da Senhora do Monte for a stunning free sunset viewpoint over the city. Bring a cold beer or wine from a nearby mini-market (€1–2) and enjoy the view with locals. Then head to a nearby tasca for dinner.

meals.breakfast: Coffee and pastel de nata at a local padaria (bakery) near the hotel — budget €2–3.
meals.lunch: Grab a bifana or caldo verde (kale soup) and bread from a market stall or snack bar near Feira da Ladra — budget €4–6.
meals.dinner: Try a simple restaurant in Mouraria or Alfama offering bacalhau à brás (shredded salt cod with eggs and potatoes) or grilled sardines. Budget €10–14 including a glass of house wine.

day_by_day.notes: Saturday mornings are ideal for the Feira da Ladra flea market — arrive by 9–10am for the best finds. Comfortable walking shoes are essential as Alfama and Mouraria involve steep cobblestone streets.

day_by_day.morning: Take the Metro or bus out to Belém (approximately 30 minutes from the city centre, covered by your transport card). Visit the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking example of Manueline architecture. Entry to the cloisters is €10; the church is free. Explore the ornate cloisters and the tomb of explorer Vasco da Gama.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk along the Belém waterfront to the iconic Torre de Belém (Tower of Belém), another UNESCO World Heritage Site. Entry is €6. Nearby, see the Monument to the Discoveries (exterior viewing is free). Then make the essential stop at the original Pastéis de Belém bakery — the birthplace of the pastel de nata — for the famous custard tarts at ~€1.30 each.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and explore the Chiado neighbourhood. Window-shop along Rua Garrett, visit the historic Bertrand Bookshop (the world's oldest operating bookshop, free entry), and enjoy the lively evening atmosphere of Largo do Chiado square.

meals.breakfast: Coffee and toast at a café near the hotel before heading out — budget €2–3.
meals.lunch: Eat at a local restaurant in Belém away from the main tourist strip. Look for a prato do dia — budget €8–10. Alternatively, pick up a fresh sandwich and eat by the Tagus riverfront.
meals.dinner: Head to Mercado de Campo de Ourique (a local food market hall popular with Lisboetas) for a budget-friendly dinner with variety — budget €10–15. Take the tram or bus from Chiado.

day_by_day.notes: Jerónimos Monastery is free on Sundays until 14:00 for EU citizens — check current policy before visiting as this may change. Arrive early to beat Sunday crowds. The Belém experience pairs perfectly with the available 'Belém Historical Monuments & Pastéis de Belém' experience listed for this trip.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — a must for history lovers. Housed in a stunning former convent, it traces the 500-year history of Portugal's iconic azulejo tiles. Entry is €5 (free on the first Sunday of each month). The museum is easily reached by bus from the city centre.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon in Cais do Sodré for the featured food tour experience. This iconic food hall brings together Lisbon's best chefs and traditional flavours under one roof. Even on a budget, you can graze on small dishes — try a bifana, ginjinha (sour cherry liqueur), fresh seafood, or a pastel de nata. Budget around €15–20 for a satisfying food exploration session.
day_by_day.evening: Explore the Bairro Alto neighbourhood as it comes alive in the evening. This is Lisbon's bohemian quarter, full of cheap bars, independent shops, and casual eateries. Enjoy a ginjinha at a street kiosk (~€1.50) and find a petiscos (Portuguese tapas) bar for a relaxed dinner.

meals.breakfast: Coffee and a tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese sandwich) at a local café — budget €3–4.
meals.lunch: The Time Out Market is your afternoon activity — graze on 3–4 small dishes or snacks here as your main midday meal. Budget €15–20.
meals.dinner: Petiscos dinner in Bairro Alto — order several small sharing plates such as pataniscas de bacalhau (salt cod fritters), presunto (cured ham), and queijo (cheese) with wine. Budget €12–16.

day_by_day.notes: The Time Out Market is busiest at lunch and dinner — visiting in the afternoon (around 15:00–17:00) means shorter queues and a more relaxed experience. This day covers the 'Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour' experience from the available activities list.

day_by_day.morning: Explore the Príncipe Real neighbourhood — one of Lisbon's most elegant and leafy districts. Visit the Jardim do Príncipe Real (a lovely free garden with a giant cedar tree) and browse the Monday/Tuesday antiques and organic market. Wander past the beautiful 19th-century mansions and independent boutiques.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the free Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara viewpoint in Bairro Alto for a final panoramic view over the city. Then take the historic Elevador da Glória (funicular, covered by transport card) down to Restauradores. Spend your last afternoon revisiting any favourite spots, picking up affordable souvenirs such as local wine (~€5–8), tinned fish (conservas, ~€3–6), or ceramic tiles from neighbourhood shops rather than tourist traps.
day_by_day.evening: Enjoy a final leisurely dinner in Baixa or Mouraria. Raise a glass of vinho verde (young Portuguese wine) to a wonderful Lisbon trip. Pack and prepare for departure.

meals.breakfast: A proper sit-down café breakfast — coffee, fresh orange juice, and a croissant or tosta — at a local café in Príncipe Real. Budget €4–6.
meals.lunch: Visit a local tasca in Príncipe Real or Bairro Alto for a prato do dia — budget €8–10. Try açorda (bread-based soup) or cozido à portuguesa if available.
meals.dinner: Final dinner at a neighbourhood restaurant in Mouraria or Baixa. Splurge slightly on your last night — grilled fish (peixe grelhado) or a traditional carne de porco à alentejana (pork with clams). Budget €14–18 including wine.

day_by_day.notes: Keep your Viva Viagem transport card topped up for the return journey to the airport. The Metro Red Line from Baixa-Chiado (change at Alameda) or Green Line connects to the airport. Allow at least 1.5–2 hours before your flight for the journey and check-in. Total estimated daily budget: €40–60 per person including transport, entry fees, and meals.

trip_options.title: Classic Lisbon, Portugal Experience
trip_options.description: The sweet spot between comfort and value. Enjoy quality accommodations, diverse experiences, and good food.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Collect luggage, clear customs, and take the Aerobus or Metro (Red Line to Green Line) into the city center. Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a leisurely self-guided stroll through the Chiado and Baixa neighborhoods — Lisbon's elegant downtown grid rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake. Walk along Rua Augusta, pass through Praça do Comércio by the Tagus riverfront, and soak in the city atmosphere. Stop at a local pastelaria for your first pastel de nata.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon (Mercado da Ribeira) for a relaxed first dinner. Graze through stalls from award-winning local chefs — try bacalhau (salt cod), prego (steak sandwich), and fresh seafood. A perfect low-key introduction to Lisbon's food scene.

meals.breakfast: Grab a coffee and croissant at the airport or on arrival — nothing formal scheduled before check-in.
meals.lunch: Light snack near the hotel upon arrival — try a local café for a tosta mista (ham and cheese toastie) and galão coffee (€4–6).
meals.dinner: Time Out Market Lisbon — budget €15–25 per person for a satisfying mix of Portuguese dishes and a glass of local wine.

day_by_day.notes: Keep Day 1 light — jet lag and travel fatigue are real. Pick up a Lisboa Card at the airport or a metro station for unlimited transport and museum discounts over the coming days. The Baixa stroll is flat and easy, ideal for a first afternoon.

day_by_day.morning: Start the day with the Alfama District Walking Tour. Join a guided group tour through Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood — wind through narrow cobblestone streets, visit the Sé Cathedral (Lisbon's oldest church, founded 1147), and climb to the Miradouro das Portas do Sol viewpoint for sweeping views over terracotta rooftops and the Tagus River.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue exploring Alfama independently after the tour. Visit the São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) — a Moorish hilltop fortress with panoramic city views and fascinating archaeological ruins. Spend 1.5–2 hours exploring the ramparts and towers. Descend via the winding streets and browse local ceramic and azulejo tile shops.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Alfama for the Fado Show experience. Dine at a traditional tasca (tavern) and enjoy a live Fado performance — Portugal's soulful, UNESCO-recognized musical tradition born right here in Alfama. This is an unmissable cultural highlight of any Lisbon visit.

meals.breakfast: At your hotel or a nearby café — coffee, fresh bread with butter and jam, and a pastel de nata (€4–7).
meals.lunch: A Tasca do Chico or similar local tasca in Alfama — try caldo verde (kale soup), grilled sardines or bacalhau à brás. Expect €12–18 per person.
meals.dinner: Fado restaurant in Alfama such as Mesa de Frades or Sr. Fado — prix-fixe dinner with Fado show typically €35–50 per person including wine. Book in advance.

day_by_day.notes: Wear comfortable shoes — Alfama's cobblestones are steep and uneven. The walking tour typically starts around 10:00; book online the evening before. Fado shows usually begin at 20:00 or 21:00 — reservations are strongly recommended, especially on weekends.

day_by_day.morning: Full day dedicated to Belém. Take Tram 15E or the train from Cais do Sodré westward to Belém (20–30 minutes). Begin at the Jerónimos Monastery — a breathtaking UNESCO World Heritage Site and masterpiece of Manueline architecture, built to celebrate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India. Explore the ornate cloisters and the church where da Gama is buried. Allow 1.5–2 hours.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk to the iconic Tower of Belém (Torre de Belém), a 16th-century fortified tower rising from the Tagus riverbank — another UNESCO-listed Manueline gem. Nearby, visit the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos), a dramatic riverside sculpture honoring Portugal's Age of Exploration. Stroll along the Belém waterfront promenade.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and explore the Bairro Alto neighborhood — Lisbon's bohemian hilltop quarter. Browse independent shops and galleries in the early evening, then settle into one of the neighborhood's lively wine bars or tascas for dinner and a nightcap.

meals.breakfast: Stop at the legendary Pastéis de Belém bakery (open since 1837) right next to the Jerónimos Monastery — the original pastel de Belém with cinnamon and powdered sugar is a must (€1.50 each). Coffee included.
meals.lunch: Picnic-style lunch on the Belém waterfront — grab fresh bread, local cheese, cured meats, and fruit from a nearby deli or supermarket (€8–12). Alternatively, Solar dos Presuntos-style casual restaurant near Belém (€15–20).
meals.dinner: Bairro Alto — try Taberna da Rua das Flores or Zé da Mouraria style taverna for petiscos (Portuguese tapas) and natural wine. Budget €20–30 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is best visited on a weekday to avoid weekend crowds. Purchase Jerónimos Monastery tickets online in advance to skip queues. The Lisboa Card covers entry to both the Monastery and the Tower of Belém — excellent value. Belém is approximately 6 km west of central Lisbon.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Museum of Ancient Art (Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga) — Portugal's most important art museum, housing masterpieces including Hieronymus Bosch's 'The Temptation of St. Anthony' triptych and an extraordinary collection of Portuguese gold and silverwork, Asian artifacts from the Age of Discoveries, and 15th–19th century European paintings. Allow 2–2.5 hours.
day_by_day.afternoon: Join the Mouraria Neighborhood Food & History Walk. Discover Lisbon's multicultural Mouraria quarter — the ancient Moorish district and true birthplace of Fado music. A guided food walk combines history (the neighborhood predates the Christian reconquest of 1147) with tastings of traditional Portuguese snacks, local wines, and street food from the neighborhood's diverse immigrant communities.
day_by_day.evening: End the day in the lively LX Factory — a repurposed 19th-century industrial complex in Alcântara now filled with restaurants, bars, concept stores, and street art. On Tuesday evenings it has a relaxed atmosphere perfect for dinner and drinks. Alternatively, return to Chiado for a quiet dinner and a stroll past the iconic Brasileira café where Fernando Pessoa's statue sits.

meals.breakfast: Hotel breakfast or a café near the museum — galão, toast, and fruit (€5–8).
meals.lunch: Tastings included in the Mouraria Food Walk (typically 6–8 stops). Supplement with a sit-down petisco if still hungry — budget €5–10 extra.
meals.dinner: LX Factory — try O Corvo or a similar mid-range restaurant. Expect €20–30 per person for a full meal with wine.

day_by_day.notes: The Mouraria Food & History Walk typically runs 3–3.5 hours and covers about 2 km on foot. Book in advance as group sizes are limited. The National Museum of Ancient Art is closed on Mondays — Tuesday is ideal. The Lisboa Card provides free or discounted entry.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Museu do Azulejo (National Tile Museum) — a unique and beautiful museum dedicated to Portugal's iconic azulejo ceramic tile tradition, housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. The highlight is a 23-metre panoramic tile panel depicting pre-earthquake Lisbon (circa 1738). Allow 1.5–2 hours. Afterward, browse the Intendente neighborhood nearby for local street art and independent cafés.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Chiado for a final afternoon of exploration — visit the São Carlos National Theatre, browse the bookshops on Rua do Carmo, and take the iconic Elevador de Santa Justa (a 19th-century iron lift) up to the Bairro Alto for one last panoramic view over the city. Visit any remaining sights or shops and pick up souvenirs: local wines, tinned fish (conservas), and ceramic tiles make excellent gifts.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at a classic Lisbon restaurant. Splurge slightly on your last night — try a traditional Portuguese restaurant in Chiado or Príncipe Real for grilled fish, arroz de marisco (seafood rice), or a classic bacalhau dish paired with a bottle of Alentejo red or Vinho Verde white.

meals.breakfast: A proper sit-down café breakfast in Intendente or near the Tile Museum — eggs, toast, fresh orange juice, and coffee (€6–10).
meals.lunch: Light lunch in Chiado — a sandwich from Mercearia do Chiado or a soup and salad at a local café (€8–12).
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Taberna Albricoque, Cervejaria Ramiro (seafood), or Tasca do Chico — budget €30–45 per person for a memorable final meal with wine and dessert.

day_by_day.notes: The Tile Museum (Museu do Azulejo) is located slightly east of the city center — take the 794 bus or a short Uber ride. It is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays, so Wednesday is perfect. If departing the following morning, pack bags the night before and confirm airport transport. The Lisboa Card expires after 72 hours — time its purchase accordingly.

highlights: Mix of paid and free experiences

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Private airport transfer arranged to Lisbon City Stay hotel. Check-in, freshen up, and settle into your luxury accommodations.
day_by_day.afternoon: After check-in, take a leisurely stroll through the elegant Chiado and Bairro Alto neighborhoods near the hotel. Browse the iconic Livraria Bertrand (world's oldest operating bookshop) and soak in the atmosphere of Largo do Chiado square. Stop at a traditional pastelaria for your first taste of Lisbon.
day_by_day.evening: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour — spend the early evening grazing through Lisbon's iconic food hall at Mercado da Ribeira, sampling dishes from the city's best chefs including fresh seafood, petiscos, and traditional Portuguese delicacies. A perfect introduction to Lisbon's culinary scene.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast on the plane or at the airport upon arrival — no hotel breakfast on Day 1.
meals.lunch: Light meal at the hotel or a quick stop at Café A Brasileira in Chiado, one of Lisbon's most historic and beloved coffee houses — try the bifanas or a classic tosta mista.
meals.dinner: Dine at Belcanto (2 Michelin stars, Chef José Avillez) in Chiado — Portugal's most celebrated fine dining restaurant offering a tasting menu rooted in Portuguese culinary heritage. Reservations essential and highly recommended well in advance.

day_by_day.notes: Flight arrives at 13:00 local time (Western European Summer Time, UTC+1). Arrange a private luxury transfer in advance. Chiado is walkable from most central Lisbon hotels. Belcanto reservations should be booked weeks ahead — confirm before travel.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Historical Monuments & Pastéis de Belém — depart early by private car or taxi to Belém (approx. 20 minutes west of the city center). Begin with a guided visit to the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking masterpiece of Manueline Gothic architecture. Explore the ornate cloisters and the tombs of Vasco da Gama and Luís de Camões.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue in Belém with a visit to the iconic Tower of Belém (Torre de Belém) on the banks of the Tagus River, followed by the nearby Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos). Enjoy sweeping riverside views. Stop at the legendary Pastéis de Belém bakery (since 1837) for the original and authentic pastel de nata — a non-negotiable Lisbon experience.
day_by_day.evening: Return to the city center and enjoy a relaxing evening in the Príncipe Real neighborhood — one of Lisbon's most refined and upscale quarters. Browse antique shops, the Príncipe Real Garden, and prepare for a memorable dinner.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel — enjoy a full Portuguese breakfast with fresh bread, local cheeses, presunto (cured ham), and fresh-squeezed orange juice.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Feitoria Restaurant (1 Michelin star) inside the Altis Belém Hotel & Spa, overlooking the Tagus River — an elegant setting with a creative Portuguese tasting menu featuring seasonal and local ingredients.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Tasca do Chico in Príncipe Real or the refined Largo restaurant inside the Chiado's historic convent — contemporary Portuguese cuisine in a stunning setting with an exceptional wine list featuring Douro and Alentejo labels.

day_by_day.notes: Belém can be reached by Uber, taxi, or the iconic Tram 15E (though private transfer is recommended for a premium experience). The Jerónimos Monastery can be crowded on weekends — arrive early (opening time ~10:00) to beat the crowds. Wear comfortable shoes for cobblestone walking.

day_by_day.morning: Alfama District Walking Tour & Fado Show (morning portion) — join a premium private guided walking tour through Alfama, Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood. Wind through narrow cobblestone streets, past Moorish-influenced architecture, colorful azulejo-tiled facades, and hidden miradouros (viewpoints). Visit the majestic São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) for panoramic views over the city and the Tagus.
day_by_day.afternoon: Mouraria Neighborhood Food & History Walk — descend from Alfama into the adjacent Mouraria quarter, the historic birthplace of Fado music and Lisbon's most multicultural neighborhood. A knowledgeable local guide will lead you through its layered history — from Moorish occupation to modern immigrant communities — with tastings of local street food, spices, and traditional bites along the way.
day_by_day.evening: Experience a world-class Fado show — the culmination of your Alfama and Mouraria explorations. Attend an intimate, authentic Fado performance at one of Lisbon's finest Fado houses for an emotionally powerful evening of Portugal's soulful musical tradition.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel followed by a coffee stop at one of Alfama's charming local cafés at the start of the walking tour.
meals.lunch: Lunch during the Mouraria Food & History Walk — guided tastings and a sit-down meal at a curated local restaurant in Mouraria, sampling dishes like caldo verde, bacalhau à Brás, and grilled sardines.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Sr. Fado or Clube de Fado in Alfama — both are renowned premium Fado restaurants combining exceptional traditional Portuguese cuisine (grilled fish, slow-cooked meats, petiscos) with live Fado performances in an intimate setting. Dinner and show combined.

day_by_day.notes: The Alfama walking tour and Mouraria walk can be combined as a full-day private guided experience — coordinate with your concierge for a seamless booking. Fado restaurants fill up quickly on weekends; reservations are mandatory. Comfortable walking shoes are essential for the steep, uneven streets of Alfama.

day_by_day.morning: National Museum of Ancient Art & Chiado Exploration — begin the morning at the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (MNAA), Portugal's most important art museum. Housed in a 17th-century palace overlooking the Tagus, it holds masterpieces including Hieronymus Bosch's 'The Temptation of Saint Anthony,' Nuno Gonçalves' iconic polyptych panels, and an extraordinary collection of Portuguese decorative arts, gold, and azulejos.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Chiado neighborhood in depth — visit the Museu do Chiado (National Museum of Contemporary Art) for a contrast of modern Portuguese art, then wander through the elegant boutiques, concept stores, and galleries that line Rua Garrett and surrounding streets. Consider a visit to the stunning São Carlos National Theatre building from the outside and the nearby Igreja do Carmo (roofless Gothic church turned archaeological museum).
day_by_day.evening: Sunset drinks at a rooftop bar with panoramic city views — the TOPO Chiado or Sky Bar at the Bairro Alto Hotel offer spectacular vistas over Lisbon's terracotta rooftops and the Tagus. Follow with a refined dinner in the upscale Lapa or Santos neighborhood.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel, followed by a mid-morning espresso and pastel de nata at Manteigaria in Chiado — one of the city's finest pastelarias.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Alma (1 Michelin star, Chef Henrique Sá Pessoa) in Chiado — sophisticated modern Portuguese cuisine with a deep respect for traditional flavors and premium seasonal ingredients.
meals.dinner: Dinner at A Cevicheria or Taberna da Rua das Flores — both are beloved by Lisbon's culinary elite. Taberna da Rua das Flores offers a rotating blackboard menu of elevated traditional Portuguese petiscos and sharing plates in a warm, intimate setting. Pair with a selection from their outstanding natural and Portuguese wine list.

day_by_day.notes: The MNAA is closed on Mondays in some seasons — verify opening hours in advance and adjust to Tuesday if needed. The Chiado area is highly walkable and connects seamlessly to Bairro Alto and Príncipe Real. The rooftop bars can be busy; consider making a reservation for sunset drinks.

day_by_day.morning: Day trip or morning excursion to Sintra — just 40 minutes from Lisbon by private car, the UNESCO World Heritage town of Sintra is an unmissable experience. Visit the fairy-tale Pena Palace (Palácio da Pena) perched dramatically on a forested hilltop, and wander through the lush romantic gardens. Optionally include a brief visit to the Moorish Castle (Castelo dos Mouros) for sweeping Atlantic views.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Lisbon by early afternoon. Spend a leisurely final afternoon in the Príncipe Real and Estrela neighborhoods — visit the beautiful Basílica da Estrela and the English Cemetery, stroll through the Jardim da Estrela park, and enjoy some last-minute luxury shopping or browsing at concept stores and Portuguese artisan boutiques in Príncipe Real.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner — celebrate your final evening in Lisbon with a truly special meal at one of the city's most prestigious restaurants, followed by a nightcap at a classic Lisbon bar.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at the hotel before departing for Sintra — fuel up with a full Portuguese spread.
meals.lunch: Lunch in Sintra at Incomum by Luis Santos — a refined restaurant in the historic center of Sintra offering creative Portuguese cuisine with local Sintra ingredients including the famous queijadas (cheese pastries) and travesseiros for dessert.
meals.dinner: Grand farewell dinner at Eleven Restaurant (1 Michelin star) atop Parque Eduardo VII — panoramic glass-walled dining room with sweeping views over Lisbon and the Tagus, offering an impeccable modern European tasting menu with strong Portuguese influences. An unforgettable final evening in the city.

day_by_day.notes: A private driver for the Sintra excursion is strongly recommended over public transport for a premium experience — it allows flexibility and comfort. Book Pena Palace tickets online in advance to avoid queues. Confirm hotel checkout time and arrange late checkout or luggage storage if your departure flight is in the evening. Eleven restaurant requires advance reservations.
